excerpt_original: Sleepy Paradise Photography project — Cuba As I was photographing Cuba, I gradually began to wonder what it might be like to live there. […] Cet article Hélène Havard est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .

blocks.text: As I was photographing Cuba, I gradually began to wonder what it might be like to live there. I imagined myself in the shoes of someone who lives there, wondering how I would feel if I had to live in that environment, with that sense of confinement and the feeling that leaving or changing my life might be difficult.
I then asked myself how I might manage to live in such a world. How could I make my everyday life more beautiful? How could I transform my surroundings so that I could feel at ease there?

It was from these questions that I began to rework the colours in my photographs, giving them pastel tones. I wanted to repaint these places in my own way, as if I could alter the colours of the world around me to make it gentler, more pleasing to the eye and perhaps easier to live in.

Little by little, this transformation became a way of imagining another reality. Not by actually changing what surrounded me, but by changing the way I saw it. As if, to manage to live in a place where I felt trapped, I needed to reinvent it in my mind, to create a form of beauty there that would help me cope better with that reality.

But behind these soft colours, there is also something more melancholic. This idea of a paradise we build for ourselves, a dream we cling to in order to make everyday life more bearable, but which doesn’t necessarily allow us to change things. And then there’s the possibility that the dream will gradually slip away, that the hope of another life or another future will eventually fade with time.

With *Sleepy Paradise*, I wanted to explore this relationship between the world we live in and the one we create within ourselves. This way we have of transforming our environment through imagination, of making it more beautiful in our minds when we cannot necessarily change it in reality.

Through pastel colours, I have sought to convey this personal projection onto Cuba – caught between the desire to make the world a more beautiful place and the question of what it means to have to transform it mentally in order to be able to live there.
